title: The psychology of queues
text: Unoccupied time feels {{1}} than occupied time, and every queue is a laboratory of the difference. The famous Houston airport fix — moving baggage claim further from the gates rather than {{2}} the bags faster — cut complaints to near zero without shortening the actual wait, because waiting that is spent walking does not {{3}} as waiting. Research on queues {{4}} a set of principles: fairness matters more than speed, since people would rather wait nine minutes in an orderly line than five watching others push ahead; uncertainty inflates suffering, so a wait with no known length {{5}} worse than a longer one with a countdown; and unexplained delays anger people disproportionately, which is why a simple apology {{6}} measurable calm. The deepest finding concerns attention: discomfort fades when attention is {{7}} elsewhere, which is why lift lobbies got mirrors — people occupied by their own reflection forget to {{8}} about the wait. Queue design, in other words, is not about minutes at all. It is about what the mind is given to do while the clock runs.

gaps.explanation: 'unoccupied time feels longer' — seems to take more time; latter refers to the second of two things mentioned.
'rather than processing the bags faster' — handling them through the system; profess = claim.
'does not register as waiting' — is not experienced or recorded as such; rummage = search untidily.
'research distils a set of principles' — reduces the findings to their essence; dismantle = take apart.
'a wait with no known length feels worse' — seems; the linking verb is needed before the comparative.
'an apology buys measurable calm' — obtains it in exchange for the words; buoy = keep afloat.
'when attention is directed elsewhere' — pointed somewhere else; dedicate takes 'to'.
'forget to grumble about the wait' — complain under the breath; grapple = wrestle (with), goad = provoke.
